\section{Pooled reference-set expansion (E2c)}
The frozen reference set was built by scoring a capped 2026-08-14 pool with the documented rule (gene $+3$, variant $+5$, disease $+1$, threshold $>4$). Re-applying that same rule to the pooled candidate lists of all ten recorded systems (11,161 candidate papers) judges 313 further papers relevant on 15 variants, enlarging the reference set from 822 to 1135 papers. Every system contributes to the pool, so no single system is favoured; the judgments are title-based, exactly like the frozen set. Table~\ref{tab:supp-expansion} shows that the manuscript's headline contrasts survive the expansion.

\section{Deconfounding the M2--M3 contrast (E1)}

Rebuilding both pools through the *same* code path turns the comparison into a symmetric $2\times2$ factorial (translation $\times$ ranking) over the frozen candidate lists. Three findings matter for the manuscript. (i)~Ranking is a real effect: dedup $+$ lexical ranking lifts Recall@20 from 0.153 to 0.218 on the multi-source pool. (ii)~Translation is the dominant shallow-ranking effect and it is now measured with the ranking stage held fixed: $+0.088$ Recall@20 at the lexical rung and $+0.127$ at the reranked rung, with SetRecall unchanged ($-0.007$), i.e. translation changes *which* papers are reachable rather than how many (German 11/13, French 10/11). (iii)~The title-only cross-encoder does not help this reference set: $-0.066$ Recall@20 on the multi-source pool (Holm-significant) and $-0.027$ on the translated pool (not significant after correction); the interaction term is $+0.039$. Because reference-set membership itself requires an explicit variant mention, exact-match lexical ranking is structurally advantaged; the ClinVar comparison below provides the independent check. One artifact caveat is reported rather than silently fixed: the recorded M3 permutation is not reproducible by re-applying the documented ranker to the stored M3 list (Recall@20 0.276 recorded vs 0.306 re-ranked), so both orders are reported and the recorded one is kept for continuity with the manuscript's table.
\section{Offline language backfill (E4a)}
305 of 822 reference papers had no provider language label. A deterministic classifier (Unicode script detection plus weighted function/domain vocabulary and orthographic markers; English as the competing hypothesis) recovers a label for 300 of them, leaving 5 undecided. Thresholds were selected on a calibration half of the provider-labelled papers and are reported on a held-out half: accuracy 0.984, non-English precision 0.933 and recall 0.933. The audit also exposes 8 provider labels contradicted by evidence (non-Latin-script titles, or journals written in the detected language), e.g.\\ five Chinese articles labelled \code{en}. Backfilling raises the German bucket from 13 to 18 papers and the French from 11 to 20.

\section{Independent truth: ClinVar submitter citations (E2a)}
To remove this project from the truth loop we collected the literature that clinical laboratories cite when they submit a variant interpretation to ClinVar (\code{esearch}/\code{esummary} on ClinVar, \code{elink} to PubMed, generic guidelines removed by a cross-variant filter). Records were found for 36 of 43 variants, yielding 3,275 curated citations. The systems' candidate pools contain 358 of the 3,275 (variant, paper) matches, so absolute recall is bounded by pool reach rather than by the reference set.

The result is a negative one, and it is reported as such: on this independent truth the pipeline does \emph{not} outperform PubMed-only, and the federated multi-source configuration does slightly better than M4n. The reason is temporal, not methodological: the curated citations have median year 2011 (34% from 2015 onward), whereas the retrieved pools have median year 2025 (89% from 2015 onward). ClinVar citations are the historical evidence base for a variant (functional studies, older cohorts, segregation analyses); the benchmark queries and the providers skew recent. The two evaluations therefore measure different things --- recency-weighted reach (manuscript reference set) versus historical evidence coverage (ClinVar) --- and the manuscript's claims are restricted to the former.

Two conclusions follow. Federation, not ranking, produces the set-level gain: within each track SetRecall is fixed, while across tracks it moves from 0.269 to 0.472. And on a single pool no modern ranker beats the pipeline's own lexical ranking of the federated pool --- dense, cross-encoder and multilingual-dense rankers land between the recorded order and lexical ranking on the reference set --- which is why the headline comparison in the manuscript is a set-coverage comparison and not a reranking claim.
\section{Reranking: a helper defect, corrected measurements and gating (E4c)}
While building the deconfounding experiment we found that the shared benchmark helper \code{rerank\_docs} restored the provider response to \emph{input} order (\code{sorted(..., key=index)}) and its callers then truncated with \code{[:limit]}. The recorded S2 (cross-encoder) and S3 (hybrid) baselines and the \code{rerank\_eval.json} optimization artifact therefore contain \emph{no} cross-encoder effect: their order is the unranked pool order. The helper is fixed (regression test \code{tests/test\_rerank\_ordering.py}); live re-runs of the affected baselines were not necessary because the frozen pools allow every ranker to be re-applied offline through one cached, corrected code path.
With the corrected ordering, re-ranking the nested pipeline list (M5) leaves the shallow metrics where they were (Recall@20 $+0.0001$, nDCG@20 $-0.0010$, both n.s.), whereas the citation gate (M5g: keep only citation items whose rerank score reaches the minimum score of the top-20 M3 candidates) removes the precision cost of citation traversal without losing its two relevant papers: Precision@Retrieved $+0.0103$ ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<10^{-4}$), SetRecall $-0.0016$ (n.s.), keeping 12 of 299 citation items. The gate is the recommended operating point when precision matters.

Widening the citation seed from one to five top-ranked M3 DOIs is not a free lunch: k=1 appends 151 citation papers and contributes 2 relevant ones (pooled reference set), k=3 appends 400 for 3, and k=5 appends 624 for 6, while Precision@Retrieved falls significantly at every step ($-0.0095$ and $-0.0153$ respectively, both $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.001$). The single-seed default with the gate above is the better operating point.
\section{Relevance-gate measurement (E4b)}
The benchmark ran with \code{relevance\_gate=False}, so the gate advertised in Figure~1 had no measured numbers. We ran it (production prompt) over a deterministic, variant-stratified sample of 120 candidate papers (60 reference-set papers and as many protocol-rejected candidates, so the sample prior is 50/50 and only the *rates* are interpretable), feeding PubMed abstracts through its \code{parsed\_markdown} input. The production default model (\code{gpt-5} at \code{linxi.chat}) was rate-limited (HTTP 429) throughout the measurement window, so the identical prompt was run with \code{Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct}; the substitution is recorded in the artifact and the measurement should be repeated on the production model. The gate retained 96.7% of the candidates: it dropped 2 of 60 reference-set papers (false-negative rate 0.033) and 2 of 60 rejected candidates (false-positive rate 0.967), i.e.\ on abstract-length input the gate is close to a pass-through and is not an effective precision filter; Precision@Retrieved moves from 0.500 to 0.500. Cost: 1233\,ms per paper and 1650 prompt characters on average, with no parse errors. Because a false negative removes a paper a clinician would have wanted, the gate should stay opt-in until it is measured on the production model with full-text input.
\section{Double annotation package (E2b, status: awaiting raters)}
The expert re-annotation called for in the paper is prepared as a ready-to-run package: a deterministic, disease-stratified sample of 15 variants (V003, V006, V012, V015, V017, V019, V020, V022, V025, V027, V029, V032, V036, V037, V042) and 225 papers (150 heuristic positives, 75 heuristic negatives drawn from the pooled candidates the protocol rejected), two identical blank sheets with the Level~1 (topic relevance) and Level~2 (variant-level evidence) criteria, and an analysis script that reports Cohen's $\kappa$ per level, the heuristic's precision/recall against each rater and the consensus, and the list of disagreements for adjudication. Files: \code{benchmarks/annotation/} (\code{e2b\_sample.csv}, \code{e2b\_sheet\_raterA.csv}, \code{e2b\_sheet\_raterB.csv}, \code{e2b\_key.csv}) and \code{benchmarks/analysis/e2b\_agreement.py}. The target is $\kappa\ge0.70$; the resulting numbers will replace the provisional truth used by the ClinVar and relevance-gate analyses.
